title: Hell in the Prophets
hook: Do Isaiah, Malachi and Daniel really warn of eternal torment in hellfire?
tldr: No. The prophets have no Hebrew term for hellfire. Sheol is the grave. Isaiah's enlarged Sheol and burning corpses picture national destruction that history fulfilled, Malachi's furnace is temporary purification, and Daniel's 'everlasting' shame belongs to the age to come and can lead to repentance.
big_idea: The prophets warned of earthly judgment and purification, never eternal torment.

points.title: Sheol means the grave
points.text: The prophets have no word for hellfire. Sheol, the realm of the dead, is translated grave, underworld, pit, death or hell, causing major confusion about the afterlife.

points.title: Isaiah's warnings came true
points.text: Sheol enlarging its mouth pictured the many deaths awaiting unrepentant Israel, fulfilled by Assyria in 722 BCE, Sennacherib in 701 BCE and Babylon in 586 BCE.

points.title: Dead bodies, not tortured people
points.text: Isaiah 66:24 describes corpses consumed by unquenched fire and undying worms: total, irrevocable destruction of pagan nations that will never rise again, not people ceaselessly tortured.

points.title: Malachi's furnace purifies
points.text: The burning day of Malachi 4:1 was one of Israel's many judgment days: imminent, temporary and purifying. God sits as a refiner of silver and gold.

points.title: Daniel's 'everlasting' means age-long
points.text: Olam signifies a long duration or the age to come, not infinity. Daniel's shame, felt by the living, can bring repentance and restoration, as in Ezekiel 16:63.

points.title: No hellfire in the Hebrew Bible
points.text: Eden's penalty was physical death, the Mosaic curses concern this life, and God says burning people 'never entered His mind'. A doctrine absent from the Law, Prophets and Writings is not core.

sections.h: No word for hellfire in the prophets
sections.summary: The Hebrew prophets contain no term equivalent to hellfire as later Augustinian-Calvinist theology understands it. Instead Sheol, simply the realm of the dead, is translated in English versions as grave, underworld, pit, death and hell. This inconsistency has caused significant theological confusion about the afterlife. The most popular prophetic verses used to establish hellfire are examined in turn.

In the First Temple period, Isaiah stressed moral justice and called Israel and Judah to repent of moral and social decay before it was too late. Isaiah 5:14 says Sheol has enlarged its appetite and opened its mouth beyond measure, and Jerusalem's nobility and multitude will descend. The NIV has 'Death expands its jaws', the NLV 'the grave is licking its lips', the English Revised Version 'hell hath enlarged her desire'.

Sheol here means the grave, unrelated to modern hellfire. The verse is a metaphor for imminent consequences: the grave expands to hold the many who will die if Israel does not repent. In Isaiah 5:1-7, Israel is a vineyard that failed to bear good fruit despite God's care; verses 8-23 pronounce woes on social injustice and moral decay. Did Isaiah's warning come true?

In 722 BCE, decades after Isaiah, Assyria conquered the Northern Kingdom, capturing and deporting many Israelites with great loss of life. In 701 BCE Sennacherib devastated Judah's cities, including Lachish; Jerusalem was miraculously spared. In 586 BCE Babylon destroyed Jerusalem, burned the Temple and killed or exiled much of the population, the ultimate fulfillment of Isaiah's warnings about moral and spiritual decline.

Isaiah's warnings were realized in real historical events, showing their accuracy and gravity. Isaiah 5:14's grave growing to receive many newcomers depicts the extensive death toll awaiting Israel. Sheol underscores the severity of divine consequences for persistent injustice and disobedience, but it was never understood as everlasting torturous punishment in the afterlife.

Isaiah 66:23-24 is often cited for hellfire: all mankind will bow before the Lord from New Moon to New Moon and Sabbath to Sabbath, then go out and look on the dead bodies of the rebels, whose worms will not die and whose fire will not be quenched, loathsome to all. A closer look yields a different understanding than modern eternal hellfire.

Isaiah 66 explores sovereignty, judgment and restoration. Verses 1-2: heaven is God's throne, earth His footstool; He seeks humble worship, not grand temples. Verses 3-4: hypocritical rituals condemned. Verses 5-9: a pain-free birth pictures a swift, peaceful new era. Verses 10-14: Jerusalem's peace, like a mother comforting her child. Verses 15-17: judgment on pagan nations. Verses 18-24: nations gathered and creation renewed, contrasted with unrepentant pagan nations' fate.

Unquenchable fire and undying worms are a biblical metaphor, later used in the gospels, for the total, irrevocable destruction of nations. The fire is a force humans cannot extinguish, leaving only ash and char; the worms add ongoing decay, a perpetual ruin. Crucially, Isaiah describes 'dead bodies', not 'people ceaselessly tortured'. The worms are decomposers like maggots and beetles, meaning these pagan nations or empires will not rise again.

sections.h: Malachi 4:1: the day that burns like a furnace
sections.summary: Malachi 4:1 warns that the day is coming, burning like a furnace; the arrogant and every evildoer will be stubble, with neither root nor branch left. The imagery is anchored in post-exilic Israel's moral and spiritual struggles. Israel had many such judgment days. The day is imminent and inescapable, yet temporal and purifying; prophetic fire symbolizes God purifying wickedness. Malachi 3:3 pictures God as a refiner purifying the Levites like gold and silver.

Judgment on 'all the arrogant and every evildoer' shows justice targeting all unrighteousness in the community. Returned exiles struggled with disillusionment and apathy, neglecting covenant duties. 'Neither root nor branch' means evil totally eradicated so corruption cannot return. The original audience heard a call to repentance and reform, about earthly judgments in their lifetime, not eternal damnation, a concept unfamiliar to the Israelites.

Malachi 4:1 is a warning and a promise of unpleasant but temporary purification, cleansing iniquity so the community can flourish and return to righteousness. Reading it as eternal hellfire overlooks its context. Even if it also addressed the afterlife, Israel's judgments were always temporary and purifying, so any afterlife parallel would likewise be for purification, not eternal.

Daniel, with its apocalyptic visions reflecting its era, is one of the later books of the Hebrew Bible. Daniel 12:1-2 says Michael will arise in a time of unprecedented trouble, Daniel's people written in the book will be delivered, and many who sleep in the dust will awake, some to everlasting life, some to shame and everlasting contempt. Seven points challenge reading it as eternal conscious torment.

First, Daniel is highly figurative: a statue of gold, silver, bronze, iron and clay, four beasts from the sea, a two-horned ram and a goat with a prominent horn, so it must be read symbolically. Second, 'your people' means Daniel's people, the Israelites. Third, 'many', not all, of the sleepers awaken, a selective process with varied outcomes, not a universal final judgment of heaven or hell.

The Hebrew Bible mentions several books, such as the tear-recording book of Psalm 56:8 and the 'book of remembrance' of Malachi 3:16, records of people's deeds and God's acknowledgment. In Daniel the book is likely the ledger of faithful Israelites delivered in tribulation. Since the end times began with Jesus' birth, it may allude to the catastrophes of 70-135 AD, when the temple fell and Jewish believers in Jesus were preserved.

Some scholars see allusions to Genesis 1-2 in 'dust' (afar) and 'earth' (adamah), pointing to the conflict between the seed of the woman and the serpent. In the day of the Lord, not a single apocalyptic event, Israel divides between the two seeds. Celestial imagery of sun, moon and stars symbolizes spiritual entities; those of the woman's seed will shine, rule god-like and enact justice in the New Eden or New Jerusalem.

Olam, translated everlasting or forever, generally means a lengthy duration, not infinity, a later philosophical concept. The Torah uses it of laws many Christians consider no longer binding; Jeremiah uses it of 70 years (Jeremiah 25:9), and Isaiah 32:14 and Jonah 2:6 of limited spans. Jewish tradition speaks of Olam Hazeh, this age, and Olam Haba, the age to come, so Daniel's life and shame may both describe the age to come, not endless duration.

Shame is not sharply separate from life: those who feel it must be alive, perhaps awakening shocked at their misdeeds. Unlike pride, shame recognizes wrongdoing and signals humility, remorse and repentance. In Ezekiel 16:63 God atones for those confounded by shame; the Prodigal Son's shame led to reconciliation (Luke 15:17). So Daniel's shame may be a period of repentance within renewal. These seven points challenge the simplistic Augustinian-Calvinist reading.

sections.h: Conclusion: no hellfire in the Old Testament
sections.summary: The Torah and Old Testament articulate no doctrine of hellfire; ECT proponents extrapolate from a handful of disparate verses. Eden's penalty was physical death: 'in the day that you eat of it you shall surely die' (Genesis 2:17), fulfilled by expulsion and loss of the Tree of Life. Destruction is consistently physical and immediate, as in the flood, Sodom and Gomorrah, and the defeats of Israel's enemies.

If hellfire were real, Moses would mention it. The Mosaic Covenant, with the Ten Commandments and over 600 laws, sets blessings and curses within this life (Deuteronomy 28), with no eternal torment. In Jeremiah 32:35 God condemns burning people as sacrifices to Molech as something that 'never entered His mind', a contradiction if He planned to burn most of humanity forever. A doctrine absent from the Law, Prophets and Writings is not core. So where did it originate?

sections.h: Sheol mistranslated and the road to the New Testament
sections.summary: Sheol, inconsistently translated hell, symbolizes the grave, the realm of the dead, not eternal torment. Continuing to render it hell perpetuates misunderstanding, obscures the original intent and distorts the Bible's view of the afterlife. When the gospels and letters were written, the Hebrew Scriptures were the only Bible, and Jesus and his Jewish disciples taught from them. The New Testament must be read asking whether it adds eternal hellfire or continues these themes.

mythfact.myth: When the Old Testament says hell, it means a place of fiery torment.
mythfact.fact: The word is Sheol, the realm of the dead or grave. The prophets have no term equivalent to hellfire.

mythfact.myth: Isaiah 66:24 describes the damned being tortured forever.
mythfact.fact: It describes dead bodies consumed by fire and worms, an image of nations destroyed so completely they never rise again.
Olam means a long duration or the age to come, only 'many' awake, and shame can lead to repentance and restoration.

mythfact.myth: Moses warned Israel about eternal hell.
mythfact.fact: Over 600 laws set blessings and curses for this life (Deuteronomy 28), with no mention of eternal torment.

quiz.q: What does the Hebrew word Sheol mean?
options: The realm of the dead, the grave
quiz.why: Sheol is the realm of the dead, variously translated grave, pit, death or hell.

quiz.q: What does Isaiah 66:24 describe being eaten by worms?
quiz.why: Isaiah describes dead bodies, an image of nations destroyed so they never rise again.

quiz.q: How does Jeremiah use olam, often translated everlasting?
quiz.why: Jeremiah 25:9 uses olam for 70 years, showing it means a long duration, not infinity.

reflect: If the Hebrew Scriptures never taught hellfire, where do you think the idea came from, and why did it stick?
